name: Lateral medullary syndrome
vascularTerritory: Lateral medullary vertebral and PICA branch territories; vertebral disease is a more common cause than isolated PICA occlusion.
presentation: Common features include ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss, contralateral body pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo/nystagmus, hoarseness/dysphagia and ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Symptoms depend on the nuclei and pathways involved; facial sensory patterns vary. Limb and facial motor function are usually relatively preserved, but extension can add weakness. Hiccups, nausea and autonomic disturbances can occur.
cause: Infarction of lateral medulla from vertebral/PICA territory disease, including atherosclerotic, embolic or dissection mechanisms. Similar regional lesions can have nonvascular causes.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, lateral medullary syndrome and Table 14.7, printed pp. 656-657 (PDF pp. 682-683).

name: Medial medullary syndrome
vascularTerritory: Paramedian branches of vertebral and anterior spinal arteries, with rostrocaudal variation and overlapping territories.
presentation: A lesion involving all three key structures can cause contralateral arm/leg weakness (pyramid), contralateral vibration/position loss (post-crossing medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue weakness (XII nucleus/fascicles). The full triad need not occur. In medullary medial lemniscus the lower-limb representation is predominantly ventral rather than the lateral position reached after rotation in the pons.
cause: Medial medullary infarction involving pyramidal, medial lemniscal and/or hypoglossal pathways. Lesion extent determines which components are present.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, medial medullary syndrome, printed pp. 656-657 (PDF pp. 682-683).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).

name: Hemimedullary syndrome
vascularTerritory: Combined medial and lateral medullary branch territories, sometimes with extensive vertebral artery disease; not a fixed single-artery hemisection territory.
presentation: An extensive unilateral medullary lesion can combine medial features (contralateral weakness and vibration/position loss, ipsilateral tongue weakness) with lateral features (crossed pain-temperature loss, dysphagia/hoarseness, ataxia and Horner syndrome). Individual findings and severity vary.
cause: Combined medial/lateral medullary infarction or another extensive regional lesion. Vertebral disease can compromise multiple branches but does not necessarily devascularize exactly half the medulla.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, combined medial and lateral medullary involvement, printed pp. 656-657 (PDF pp. 682-683).

name: Millard-Gubler syndrome
vascularTerritory: Paramedian basilar branches to ventral caudal pons; lesion extent and lateral spread vary.
presentation: Ventral caudal pontine lesions may combine ipsilateral facial fascicular weakness and contralateral body weakness; abducens fascicular palsy is included in some historical descriptions. A VI nerve/fascicle palsy impairs ipsilateral abduction, whereas an abducens nuclear or PPRF lesion impairs conjugate gaze. Eponym definitions vary, so the actual deficit pattern should be stated.
cause: A ventrocaudal pontine lesion affecting descending motor fibers and facial fascicles, with variable adjacent VI involvement. Causes include infarction, hemorrhage, mass or demyelination.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, Table 14.8 and medial pontine syndromes, printed pp. 658-659 (PDF pp. 684-685).

name: Foville syndrome
vascularTerritory: Paramedian basilar branches to medial caudal pontine basis and tegmentum.
presentation: The commonly described pattern combines ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy, ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness and contralateral body weakness. It involves the facial colliculus/gaze circuitry and descending motor fibers. Medial lemniscal sensory loss or INO can accompany extension; hearing loss is not a defining obligatory feature.
cause: Medial caudal pontine lesion extending from basis toward the facial colliculus, often vascular. Historical usage of the eponym varies.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, Table 14.8 and medial pontine syndromes, printed pp. 658-659 (PDF pp. 684-685).

name: Locked-in syndrome
vascularTerritory: Often bilateral ventral pontine ischemia from basilar disease; locked-in presentations also have other structural or peripheral motor causes.
presentation: Severe paralysis and loss of speech output with preserved consciousness characterize the syndrome. In a classic ventral pontine pattern, vertical eye movement or blinking is often preserved and can allow communication. Incomplete and total forms occur; sensory function and ocular movement can vary with lesion extent.
cause: Severe motor-output disconnection, classically bilateral corticospinal/corticobulbar injury in ventral pons with relatively preserved arousal circuitry. Hemorrhage, demyelination or other motor disorders can produce related presentations.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, KCC 14.1 locked-in syndrome, printed pp. 625 (PDF pp. 651).

name: Osmotic demyelination with central pontine involvement
vascularTerritory: Nonvascular osmotic/metabolic demyelination; extrapontine involvement can coexist.
presentation: Pontine involvement can cause dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, movement or ocular abnormalities, and severe cases a locked-in presentation. Symptom timing and MRI visibility vary; a fixed examination/MRI sequence is not required.
cause: Osmotic demyelination associated particularly with osmotic shifts during correction of chronic hyponatremia, with additional risk contexts such as malnutrition or liver disease. It is predominantly myelin injury rather than a selective pontine-neuron lesion.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and pontine myelinolysis, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, motor-output syndromes, printed pp. 625 (PDF pp. 651).

name: Cerebellar syndrome (dentate/SCP)
vascularTerritory: Cerebellar SCA/AICA/PICA territories overlap and vary; the clinical syndrome also has many nonvascular causes.
presentation: Cerebellar-system dysfunction can produce dysmetria, decomposition, intention tremor, impaired rapid alternating movement, dysarthria, gait/truncal ataxia or ocular motor abnormalities. Hemispheric and pre-crossing output lesions commonly affect ipsilateral limbs; lesions above crossed cerebellar output affect contralateral limbs. Midline/vestibular involvement can predominantly disturb gait, balance and eye movement.
cause: Cerebellar cortical, deep-nuclear, peduncular or connected pathway disease from infarct, hemorrhage, inflammation, toxic/metabolic injury, degeneration or mass effect.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, divisions, nuclei and pathways, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar clinical localization, printed pp. 712-721 (PDF pp. 738-747).

name: Lateral pontine syndrome
vascularTerritory: Often AICA-related lateral caudal pontine disease, with variable basilar/circumferential contributions; labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA.
presentation: May combine ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo/nystagmus, facial pain-temperature loss or facial weakness, contralateral body pain-temperature loss and Horner syndrome. Hearing loss can occur when cochlear/nerve/labyrinthine structures are involved, but is not required and is not exclusive to this one brainstem level.
cause: Lateral caudal pontine infarction, often in AICA territory, with variable cerebellar or inner-ear extension. Other regional lesions can mimic the pattern.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, Table 14.8 and AICA syndrome, printed pp. 658-659 (PDF pp. 684-685).

name: One-and-a-half syndrome
eponym: Fisher one-and-a-half syndrome (PPRF/abducens plus ipsilateral MLF)
vascularTerritory: Usually a dorsal pontine lesion; when vascular, paramedian basilar branches may be involved.
presentation: Combination of ipsilateral conjugate horizontal gaze palsy with ipsilateral INO from involvement of ipsilateral VI nuclear/PPRF circuitry and MLF. The only preserved horizontal movement may be abduction of the contralateral eye, often with nystagmus. Convergence can be preserved but varies; resting eye deviation is not mandatory.
cause: Dorsal pontine injury from infarction, demyelination, hemorrhage, mass or other disease. The gaze pattern localizes circuits but does not by itself establish an age-specific cause.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, horizontal gaze, INO and one-and-a-half syndrome, printed pp. 585-587 (PDF pp. 611-613).

name: Central Horner syndrome
vascularTerritory: Central sympathetic pathway lesions can occur in hypothalamus, brainstem or cervical/upper thoracic cord; lateral medullary vertebral/PICA territory is one vascular example.
presentation: Ipsilateral miosis, mild ptosis and variable anhidrosis reflect sympathetic pathway interruption. Anisocoria is often greater in darkness, with dilation lag possible. Central lesions may have additional crossed sensory, ataxic or motor signs; the degree/distribution of sweating loss varies.
cause: Interruption of descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers before the spinal preganglionic neurons. Infarction, demyelination, mass, trauma or cord disease are possible causes.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, sympathetic pupils and Horner syndrome, printed pp. 578-580 (PDF pp. 604-606).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, lateral medullary sympathetic involvement, printed pp. 656-657 (PDF pp. 682-683).
